objects: genome length; population size; forward simulation
conclusion: FPG and SIMUPOP are described as limited by feasible genome and population size, motivating computationally efficient approximate rescaling.
span: The main limitation of alternative forward-in-time simulators (FPG[3] and SIMUPOP [4]) is the size of genome and population that can be accommodated. A primary objective in the development of FREGENE has been computational efficiency. We implement a rescaling technique that greatly extends the feasible simulation size at the cost of some approximation.

conclusion: The simulated population is monoecious and diploid, with non-overlapping generations and optional subdivision.
scope: Population assumptions; subdivision is a setting.
span: FREGENE simulates the evolution of a monoecious, diploid, potentially subdivided, population over non-overlapping generations.

conclusion: Inputs comprise mutation, recombination, demographic and selection parameters and an initial population, typically null or inherited from a previous run.
span: Parameters characterising the mutation, recombination, demographic and selection processes, are specified by the user, via either input files or the command line. A starting population is also specified, typically either a 'null' population with no diversity, or a population that is the result of a previous run of FREGENE.

conclusion: Each generation is formed individual by individual using fitness-weighted parental sampling, recombination of parental sequences and uniformly located new mutations regardless of allelic state.
scope: Forward simulation transition, rather than posterior fitting.
span: Subsequently, each new generation is created one individual at a time. A parent is chosen at random, weighted by fitness, and a new sequence is generated by randomly recombining its two sequences. New mutations arise uniformly at random on the new sequence, regardless of current allelic status.

objects: selection coefficient s; dominance coefficient h
assumptions: a novel allele is selected with a specified probability
conclusion: Selected novel alleles receive random selection and dominance coefficients according to configured parameters.
scope: Generative coefficient distribution; not defined as a Bayesian inference prior.
span: Novel mutant alleles are under selection with a specified probability. If so, two coefficients are assigned at random according to parameters set in an input file: s, which we call the 'selection' coefficient, and hthe 'dominance' coefficient.

objects: s; h; genotype fitness; selected sites
assumptions: fitness contributions are additive across selected sites
conclusion: Derived homozygotes contribute s, heterozygotes sh and ancestral homozygotes zero, with fitness equal to one plus summed selected-site contributions.
span: The contribution to an individual's fitness at a site is sfor a derived-allele homozygote, shfor a heterozygote, and zero for an ancestral-allele homozygote. Thus, for s> 0, a site is recessive if h= 0; co-dominant if 0 <h< 1; and over-dominant if h> 1. Individual fitness is one plus the sum of these contributions over all selected sites.

conclusion: A stochastic recombination map is generated at the start and stays fixed throughout the simulation.
span: At the start of a FREGENE run, a C++ recombination object is invoked and uses the recombination parameters specified in the input file to stochastically assign recombination rates over the genome, including the locations and intensities of hotspots. The resulting 'recombination map' remains unchanged throughout the simulation.

conclusion: Parents originate from subpopulation j with backward migration probability mij, with the within-subpopulation probability completing the sum to one.
span: The population may be subdivided, in which case migration between subpopulations can occur according to arbitrary 'backward' migration rates: for an offspring in subpopulation i, its two parents are chosen from subpopulation jwith probability mij, which for i≠ jis specified by the user, and mii= 1 - ∑j≠imij.

conclusion: This version extends the earlier FREGENE with general migration and selection that can switch off randomly or be geographically restricted.
span: Since its first publication [1], FREGENE has been extended to incorporate several new features. A general migration model has now been included. Selection at a locus can be switched off at a random time, and can be geographically restricted.

conclusion: Approximate rescaling multiplies mutation, recombination, selection and migration rates by a common factor while dividing population size and generation count by that factor.
scope: Computational savings at the cost of approximation; no accuracy bound stated.
span: A scaling technique, described in [1], can lead to dramatic reductions in computing time and memory use at the cost of some approximation. Scaling involves increasing all rate parameters (mutation, recombination, selection, migration) by a common factor λ> 1, while reducing by a factor of λboth the population size and the number of generations.

span: An undesirable feature of scaling is that the output population size is reduced by a factor of λ, but FREGENE now offers an option either to output this reduced population or to run additional generations during which scaling is relaxed and the population size expands linearly from N/λto N.
